answer.rationale:
The tempting move is the one the mandate points at: memory_c2 says the low-cost vendor cut unit cost sharply and their quote alone meets the 18% target. But c2's supporting evidence is about onboarding speed and invoicing accuracy — administrative signals, not delivery reliability under load. It says nothing about on-time performance at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, and nothing about whether that prior switch involved this component class. So I want the archived record for c2 specifically to see whether delivery performance was ever measured or merely not observed to fail. Second, I want c4, because negotiation is my intended path and I am relying on it to deliver a large cut; the archived record should tell me the actual magnitude recovered ("real margin" is unquantified) and whether the benchmark leverage came from a credible alternative bid. If c4's recovery was only a few points, negotiation alone will not clear 18% and I need to know that before committing.

Intent: negotiate terms with the incumbent, using the low-cost quote as documented leverage, and explore the multi-year structure from c6 that cut unit cost without narrowing scope. This is the only direction that attacks cost without touching the physical supply path during a 14-day window on a line with zero slack. c1 supports that the incumbent integration has held across two cycles, so holding the path costs nothing in migration work. Switching primary vendor in 14 days at 94% utilization converts a cost problem into a delivery-continuity problem, and the objective explicitly forbids increasing delivery risk. add_second_source (c3) is the right long-run hedge but consumes my single decision on resilience rather than the mandated cut. defer_decision (c5) worked for a non-critical month-to-month service; this contract does not auto-renew, so deferring means running the line without a primary contract — that memory does not transfer.

Guarded scale: pursue the negotiation without pre-committing to a long multi-year lock until the c4 magnitude and c2 reliability questions are resolved, so the next review retains the option to add a second source or stage a qualified switch on a non-critical line first. Flagging the downstream risk: the 18% mandate creates pressure to treat a price quote as equivalent to a supply guarantee, and if I let cost dominate here the failure lands as line stoppage, which is far more expensive than the savings. If negotiation lands materially short of 18%, the answer is a partial cut plus a staged qualification of the second vendor — not an unqualified full switch.
